bi-report.main: Production-grade AWS QuickSight–driven analytics and reporting platform designed for large-scale educational environments, combining embedded BI, multi-tenant access control, database-driven analytics modeling, and aggressive session cost optimization.

summary.a: Embedded analytics platform fully integrated into the application UI using secure QuickSight embed flows.
summary.b: Designed for large-scale reporting workloads across around 1,000 schools and their administrative users.
summary.c: Database views, analytics modeling, and query tuning used to support high-frequency operational reporting.
summary.d: Snapshot-based rendering strategy reduced projected QuickSight session cost by approximately 90%.

system-scale.data-volume: Five years of historical incident data with hundreds of thousands of records, including operational metadata, incident classification, timestamps, school and facility information.
system-scale.usage-traffic: Thousands to tens of thousands of daily report views across approximately 30 reports and 10+ visualization types. Source data comes from ~50,000 staff checking in within a 15-minute morning window — peak ~180 RPS / 45 TPS and ~2,000 concurrent users (estimated from usage patterns, ~20x the daily average).
system-scale.user-scope: ~50,000 staff across around 1,000 schools generate the data, and thousands of administrative users view reports at school and district levels.

report-categories.attendance: Student attendance tracking, staff check-in / check-out logs, late arrival monitoring, and tardiness analytics.
report-categories.incident-monitoring: Vaccination reporting, infection tracking, facility exposure logging, and date / district / school-based aggregation.
report-categories.summary: Role-based dashboards providing school-only or district-wide analytical views depending on user scope.

data-platform.analytics-logic: Complex business rules, aggregations, and reporting transformations were implemented at the RDS layer using database views to reduce BI dataset complexity and stabilize query patterns.
data-platform.bi-layer: Simple report-specific expressions were delegated to QuickSight calculated fields, keeping the visualization layer lightweight and avoiding unnecessary duplication of heavy aggregation logic.
data-platform.platform: Reporting workloads were isolated from the transactional path through view-based models, SPICE usage, and dedicated read-oriented strategies to support operational analytics without destabilizing OLTP behavior.

performance-opt.heavy-report-opt: Expensive district-wide joins were reduced by isolating school metadata into DynamoDB and synchronizing relational metadata into a read-optimized structure.
performance-opt.spice: Daily summary reports were moved to SPICE with scheduled refresh, eliminating unnecessary real-time query load on the source database.
performance-opt.query-tuning: Composite indexes, execution plan analysis, join restructuring, and view-based query shaping reduced dashboard latency and improved overall reporting responsiveness.

design.a: Reports were built in QuickSight and embedded into the application using secure URLs generated through .NET API and Lambda orchestration.
design.b: Access control was enforced through API-level authorization, role-aware filtering, and parameterized tenant scoping for school-level and district-level users.
design.c: This architecture maintained secure multi-tenant isolation while keeping the reporting experience fully embedded.

strategy.a: QuickSight session pricing made high-frequency report access operationally expensive at scale.
strategy.b: A snapshot rendering pipeline was introduced: if a requested report snapshot already existed, the platform served the cached visual output instead of creating a new BI session.
strategy.c: Headless browser capture + S3 storage dramatically reduced session creation while preserving visual equivalence for non-interactive report scenarios.

impact.cost: Reduced projected QuickSight operating cost by approximately 90%.
impact.performance: Maintained around 3-second average dashboard response time.
impact.scale: Supported 1,000+ schools and thousands of administrative users.
impact.arc: Delivered a secure multi-tenant embedded analytics platform on AWS-native services.

header.title: SQL Tuning Advisor
header.desc: Designed and implemented an automated SQL tuning system by reverse-engineering Oracle SQL Tuning Advisor. The system analyzes slow SQL and generates optimization recommendations including SQL Profile, index suggestions, statistics fixes, and SQL rewrites.

overview.title: Overview
overview.desc1: Oracle SQL Tuning Advisor is an automated SQL performance analysis and optimization system provided by Oracle Database.
overview.desc2: This project reverse-engineered that workflow and implemented an Oracle-style SQL tuning automation framework, including task lifecycle management, advisor metadata tables, analysis modules, report generation, and SQL Profile acceptance flow.
overview.desc3: In practical terms, this can be understood as an advanced internal system that automates EXPLAIN analysis + optimizer tuning + recommendation generation.

purpose.title: Purpose
purpose.desc: The key objective of this project was not just manual SQL tuning, but automation of SQL tuning workflows: converting optimizer knowledge and performance diagnostics into a repeatable advisor system that can create, execute, analyze, and report tuning tasks.

stat.title: 1. Statistics Analysis
stat.desc: Detects stale or missing statistics that lead to incorrect execution plans.

profiling.title: 2. SQL Profiling
profiling.desc: Compares estimated vs actual row count patterns and generates profile-based recommendations to improve optimizer decision quality.

access.title: 3. Access Path Analysis
access.desc: Evaluates whether Full Scan or Index Scan is more appropriate and suggests access-path improvements.

structure.title: 4. SQL Structure Analysis
structure.desc: Detects query patterns that degrade performance and provides rewrite recommendations.

purpose.title: Purpose
purpose.desc: Implemented an Oracle-style SQL Tuning Advisor by reverse engineering internal architecture, including task lifecycle, analysis modules, recommendation logic, report generation, and SQL Profile acceptance flow.

milestone.c: • Design advisor packages, system tables, and views
milestone.d: • Build tuning task execution and report generation system

feature.e: • Expensive operation detection (NOT IN, UNION, join issues)

package.title: 1. Package Design
package.desc: The advisor was designed around multiple internal packages, following the Oracle-style separation between public APIs, internal execution logic, and low-level utility subprograms.

item1.a: • Public package that exposes the main advisor lifecycle APIs
item1.b: • Includes procedures/functions for CREATE, EXECUTE, REPORT, and ACCEPT SQL PROFILE
item1.c: • Serves as the main user-facing interface for tuning task management

item2.a: • Internal execution package responsible for the detailed analysis steps during tuning task execution
item2.b: • Encapsulates advisor workflow logic such as statistics analysis, access path analysis, and structural SQL checks
item2.c: • Separates internal execution behavior from the public package API

item3.a: • Utility package for subprograms that need lower-level implementation
item3.b: • Designed to isolate logic better suited for C/C++-level implementation
item3.c: • Helps keep advisor package logic modular and maintainable

table.title: 2. System Tables
table.desc: The advisor required dedicated system metadata tables created during DB booting, along with DBA-style views for visibility into definitions, tasks, objects, executions, and logs.

system_tables.definitions: • ADVISOR_DEFINITIONS: Stores metadata for advisor categories such as ADDM, SQL Access Advisor, Undo Advisor, SQL Tuning Advisor, and SQL Workload Manager
system_tables.tasks: • ADVISOR_TASKS: Stores and manages each advisor execution unit as a task
system_tables.objects: • ADVISOR_OBJECTS: Stores task-related objects by object_id and object_name
system_tables.logs: • ADVISOR_LOGS: Records step-by-step logging of advisor execution and tuning progress

table.footer: This metadata layer was critical for implementing task lifecycle persistence, execution traceability, and report generation

create.title: 3. Create Tuning Task
create.a: • Accepts user inputs such as sql_id, scope, task_name, time_limit, and related tuning parameters
create.b: • Generates default values for missing optional inputs
create.c: • Performs validation checks on input arguments
create.d: • Persists validated inputs and generated metadata into advisor system tables
create.e: • Establishes the initial lifecycle state of the tuning task

execute.title: 4. Execute Tuning Task
execute.desc: The execution phase was designed as a multi-step analysis pipeline that automatically inspects optimizer-related causes of SQL performance issues.

stat.a: • Detects missing or stale statistics on tables and indexes
stat.b: • Identifies cases where poor optimizer estimates may be caused by statistics quality issues

access.a: • Evaluates whether current access paths are cost-optimal with and without indexes
access.b: • Generates guidance on access path improvement
access.c: • Can recommend running SQL Access Advisor when index-oriented design changes are needed

structure.a: • Detects query patterns known to cause performance degradation at syntax / semantic analysis stage
structure.b: • Recommends replacing NOT IN with NOT EXISTS
structure.c: • Recommends replacing UNION with UNION ALL where appropriate
structure.d: • Detects datatype mismatch between indexed columns and WHERE clause predicates
structure.e: • Detects missing join conditions that indicate design mistakes or hidden Cartesian effects

report.a: • Aggregates advisor findings from execution logs, analysis output, and recommendation records
report.b: • Produces structured tuning reports for users
report.c: • Summarizes actionable items such as statistics collection, SQL rewrite, alternative plan, and SQL Profile usage
report.d: • Designed as the final user-facing output of the tuning task lifecycle

profile.a: • Supports applying approved SQL Profile recommendations to the target SQL
profile.b: • Connects advisor recommendation results to optimizer execution behavior
profile.c: • Bridges analysis output with actual runtime performance improvement

summary.a: • Public API Layer: DBMS_SQLTUNE package for task creation, execution, reporting, and SQL Profile acceptance
summary.b: • Internal Execution Layer: DBMS_SQLTUNE_INTERNAL package for advisor pipeline and analysis execution
summary.c: • Utility Layer: C/C++-oriented utility package for low-level subprogram support
summary.d: • Metadata Layer: Advisor system tables and DBA views for definitions, tasks, objects, logs, and executions
summary.e: • Recommendation Layer: Statistics, access path, structural rewrite, and SQL Profile recommendation generation<

conclusion.a: This project demonstrates more than SQL tuning itself: it demonstrates the design and implementation of an automated SQL tuning system that models advisor lifecycle, analysis workflow, metadata persistence, recommendation generation, and optimizer-facing profile application.
conclusion.b: It also highlights hands-on experience in C++, PL/SQL, database internals, optimizer behavior, and performance engineering.

erp-database.main: A project to move seven years of data managed in Excel and CSV files into a database — database design, data migration, and a DB monitoring dashboard.

summary.b: Schema designed in recurring sessions with the operations and merchandising owners.
summary.c: Migration code that bulk-inserts every accumulated file into the database.
summary.d: 16 scheduled batches keep the DB current as new files keep arriving.

domain.desc: Five domains, each with its own naming convention and lifecycle. The DB console classifies every table by these prefixes.

migration.code: Master tables loaded first, then their dependent tables grouped and run one stage at a time — each stage isolated so one failure never blocks the rest.
migration.backfill: Years of Excel/CSV loaded with idempotent UPSERT — a re-run repairs data instead of duplicating it. The same path became the daily incremental load.
migration.partition: Data loaded daily by date (sales, purchases, logs) is list-partitioned by store so no single table grows unbounded.

batch.a: 16 batches spread across the night (02:00–06:30) and an evening polling window, time-separated so heavy loads never overlap.
batch.b: Fallback logic for each failure case (missing file, changed format, and so on), plus backfill logic that always re-checks the previous day and fills in what is missing.
batch.c: A batch monitoring dashboard that surfaces the state of every job, with issue alerts and manual re-runs where operators need them.

console.usage: Reads PostgreSQL catalogs directly — row estimates, table and index size, vacuum/analyze times, database growth.
console.relation: Merges live foreign keys with documented logical relations, so the model people reason about matches what the DB enforces.
console.trace: Maps all 32 ERP tabs to the tables they read — the blast radius of a schema change is visible before it ships.
console.freshness: Status and statistics for the file storage (NAS) as well as the database.

impact.ssot: Seven years of Excel/CSV replaced by one PostgreSQL database — 97 tables across 5 domains as the system of record
impact.integrity: Consistency moved from spreadsheet discipline into keys and constraints, with per-store list partitioning keeping the largest tables in check
impact.automation: 16 batches keep the DB current — fallback and backfill recover the previous day even when a file is missing or its format changes
impact.ops: A batch dashboard for alerts and manual re-runs, plus a console covering usage, relations, tab dependencies, and NAS status

mcp-agent.main1: Built one assistant agent per ERP task and an MCP server that guides each agent to exactly its own work inside the whole system
mcp-agent.main2: Built a dashboard to monitor and manage the whole system

summary.a: One agent per ERP task such as pay rate, reorder or sample return — an assistant that performs the lookups and judgements the responsible team member used to do on screen
summary.b: Per-task tool bundles served over MCP so an agent never reads the whole system. Tools outside its task appear in neither the list nor the call
summary.c: Tools call the same service functions as the screens, so the number a team member sees and the number the agent reports are the same. Data-changing tools carry a separate mark and switch
summary.d: An operations screen that shows which tools are on and which requests failed for lack of a tool, so the tool set is adjusted from what agents actually needed

flow.desc1: An agent receives a request from its task tab and connects to the endpoint matched to its task scope.
flow.desc2: What to query is decided by the LLM (Codex) — Hermes hands the tool list fetched from that endpoint to the LLM on every request, and the actual reads and writes are executed by ERP tools
flow.queue: Requests land in the agent_jobs queue and two workers claim them with SKIP LOCKED. The messages, headed by the task's system prompt, and the task name (mode) go to the Hermes gateway; 300 s limit per job, orphaned jobs requeued on restart, finished jobs kept for 7 days
flow.tools: The LLM does not memorize tools. Hermes queries tools/list on the task's /mcp/<domain>/ endpoint, receives name, description and JSON Schema, and attaches them to the LLM request as function-calling tools. A tool switched off in the admin screen drops out of that list, so the LLM cannot call it
flow.loop: Codex (the LLM) reads the system prompt, the question and the tool descriptions, then decides which tool to call with which arguments. Hermes forwards the call to ERP via tools/call and puts the JSON result back into the LLM context. If the result is insufficient the LLM calls another tool; if sufficient it writes the answer. Up to 60 turns, with a warning and stop on repeated failures
flow.scope: The mode carried in the request makes Hermes show the LLM only that task's tool bundle. Questions from Telegram or Mattermost pass through the same gateway and tools, so wherever a team member asks, the answer rests on the same ERP tools

server.desc: The MCP server is the map handed to each agent. Tools are defined in a registry, exposure is decided in a catalog, and endpoints are mounted per task. A tool defined but not exposed is not on the map
server.l1: Per-task TOOL_DEFINITIONS (JSON Schema) and a dispatch function that call the service functions the screens already use, sharing the same formulas
server.l2: Only (task, tool) pairs on the EXPOSED list are visible. Write tools carry a mutating flag and warning prefix, and responses are clipped at 24,000 characters so nothing beyond need is read
server.l3: The low-level MCP Server served over Streamable HTTP (stateless, JSON responses) with Bearer token checks, excluded from cookie authentication
server.l4: Task list derived automatically from the catalog and /mcp/<domain>/ mounted one per task. The all-task /mcp/ remains only for cross-task work
server.catalog: All 13 tasks share one file layout, so a new task's agent reaches the map with one registry file and a few catalog lines. The 28 write tools can each be switched off from the admin screen

graph.desc: An agent covering every task would have to read close to 100 tools on every request. Splitting nodes by task and attaching only that task's tools lets each agent find exactly its own work. Only questions spanning two tasks go to the hub
graph.hub: The dashboard agent that sees every task's tools. Questions involving two or more tasks are handled here, where the order of tool calls is decided
graph.node: Each node has its own system prompt, tool bundle, dedicated endpoint and tab permission. Tools outside its task are blocked from both the list and the call
graph.write: Tools that change real data or builds. Marked as writes in name and description, and individually switchable per node from the admin screen
graph.pipeline: Work that needs a fixed order is registered as a job handler: collect posts → chunk → call per chunk → validate → merge, plus scheduled store summaries
graph.edge: Edges between nodes are shared service functions and database tables. Adding a node takes three registrations (registry, catalog, gateway), and a formula change on an edge is verified on both nodes

monitor.desc: An agent monitoring dashboard: which tools are active, which requests failed for lack of a tool, the load on the app hosting the MCP server and whether the gateway is alive, all checked from the ERP admin tab where the tool set is adjusted
monitor.tools: Per-task tool_count, enabled_count and mutating counts, with per-tool on/off stored in the database. Disabled tools are excluded from both listing and calls
monitor.usage: The gateway pushes model usage, plan and platform connection state every 10 minutes. A stale warning appears after 25 minutes without an update
monitor.missing: Requests the agent could not handle and calls to unregistered tools are stored with a status that admins move through review and adoption
monitor.restart: ERP never touches containers directly. A restart request is queued, a host cron claims it every minute, runs it and reports the result back. 5-minute cooldown
monitor.signals: Underneath, an admin-started Four Golden Signals session (latency, traffic, errors, saturation in 10 s buckets, 14-day retention) records in-flight requests, DB pool, event-loop lag and memory of the app process hosting the MCP server, and per-task agent queue stats show queued and running jobs

impact.efficiency: Each agent reads only its own task's tools, so per-request context is fixed to one task rather than the whole system. Wandering into unrelated areas is removed structurally
impact.safety: Double task-scope checks, write-tool marking, per-tool switches and Bearer authentication narrow the agent's blast radius
impact.extensibility: A new task agent is one file and a few registrations. More team members or more channels change nothing in the ERP structure
impact.observability: Tool state, usage, missing tools and restarts on one screen, with the fault-isolation order (gateway registration → catalog → execution path) fixed as a rule

agent-platform.main: Built an AI development environment spanning harness, skills, hooks, tests and specialized sub-agents, then shipped it as a marketplace plugin, implementing a system that manages development rules and workflows at team level

dist.desc: Packaged the environment into a GitHub team marketplace rather than leaving it as personal configuration, so two commands apply the same rules, agents and verification procedures
dist.install: Marketplace manifests published for both Claude Code and Codex so the same plugin installs regardless of runtime, with a SessionStart hook injecting shared development policy into new sessions
dist.erp: For developers. Mirrors the repository assets and adds team entry points — menu, project setup, team verification — plus shared policy skills
dist.db: For non-developer roles. A Korean read-only query channel requiring only a database name and account, also built as an .mcpb desktop extension for Claude Desktop users
dist.sync: The repository .claude/ directory remains the single source of truth, mirrored to the plugin by hook on edit

summary.a: Separated into context, policy, enforcement and execution layers so rule errors and enforcement gaps are fixed at independent points
summary.b: 25 hooks placed immediately before tool calls to block unapproved edits, irreversible commands and production access at execution time
summary.c: One dedicated agent per subtab, each owning its files, API endpoints, DB tables and business rules at path level
summary.d: Authoring and verification separated into distinct lanes, with 9 design and review agents kept read-only to structurally prevent self-approval

layers.desc: A structure where upper layers cannot function once a lower layer breaks, assigning rule errors to Layer 1 and enforcement gaps to Layer 3
layers.l1: Policy loaded at every session start, plus domain knowledge injected by request keyword
layers.l2: Denied, confirm-required and allowed tiers declared per command pattern
layers.l3: Executables enforcing the declaration, blocking or warning immediately before a tool call
layers.l4: Dedicated agents acting within the permitted range by reading a defined procedure

layout.desc: Identical rules and agent topology applied by repository clone alone, with no per-developer configuration

topology.desc: Ownership partitioned per subtab to remove the context overload and blurred judgment caused by a single agent covering every area
topology.design: Investigation, design and post-verification only, read-only with no implementation authority
topology.tab: Implementation ownership, with a data agent per family solely owning the backend
topology.business: Domain decisions across merchandising, ordering, returns and settlement
topology.review: Change sets isolated into a worktree and inspected in parallel across intent, quality, layer and data
topology.edge: Shared formulas and API response keys defined as edges between nodes, enabling parallel delegation of independent nodes while enforcing cross-regression checks on edge changes

hooks.desc: 25 hooks registered 28 times across 4 lifecycle events, converting recurring defect classes from documented rules into execution-time blocks
hooks.design: Editing backend or frontend without an approved design
hooks.design_o: Implementation entered with the design stage skipped
hooks.date: String bound to a date cast in asynchronous SQL
hooks.date_o: Recurring cause of 500 responses on query APIs
hooks.imported: Type convention violations on the ingestion-date column
hooks.testfile: Test files outside the requested scope included in commits
hooks.testfile_o: 859 test lines merged into a feature commit
hooks.prbase: Pull requests opened without a specified base branch
hooks.danger: Irreversible commands and production server access

permission.desc: Blast radius divided into three tiers per command pattern, graded by the cost of failure
permission.deny: Secret access and irreversible destructive commands, not releasable by approval
permission.ask: Commits, merges, container lifecycle and PR creation requiring confirmation before execution
permission.allow: Reads and searches with nothing to revert
permission.gate: Blocked operations opened temporarily through a gate file holding an expiry timestamp, granting permission as a duration rather than a state and reserving the right to open it to the user

graph.desc: Domain business rules not recoverable from code alone, split across 72 memory nodes and partially injected per request
graph.recall: Prompt and memory scored by IDF, injecting the best match within a fixed budget
graph.learn: Corrections accumulated as numbered entries in per-domain feedback files and re-injected automatically in later sessions
graph.consolidate: Unrecorded corrections and unverified completion claims checked at session exit

impact.reliability: Three recurring defect classes converted into execution-time blocks, removing their recurrence path
impact.safety: Irreversible commands and production access blocked beneath the approval layer, with access granted only through expiring gates
impact.throughput: Parallel delegation of independently owned nodes supporting concurrent multi-feature development
impact.onboarding: Identical environment applied across the team through two marketplace commands, with no per-developer setup

erp-architecture.main: An in-house ERP that automates purchasing, inventory, ordering and settlement for 10 apparel retail stores — alternatives compared against quality attributes and constraints, with the key design decisions and trade-offs documented in 8 ADRs.

summary.a: Files from vendors and POS are cleaned and evaluated overnight, then delivered as per-store order sheets (.xls) and 60 operating tabs.
summary.b: Scalability was left out of the quality goals given the system's size; accuracy and change velocity were set as the priorities.
summary.c: 8 design decisions recorded as ADRs, each with its benefits and accepted costs.
summary.d: 9 technical debt items linked to their ADRs, each with a defined review trigger.

flow.desc: Business goals were broken down into architecture drivers (core functions, quality attributes, constraints). Alternatives that met those drivers were compared at three levels — tactic, style and pattern — and the decision was made after reviewing the trade-offs. Key decisions are recorded as ADRs.

lens.desc: The three terms, using the caching decision as an example: a tactic is what to do, a pattern is how it is structured, and a trade-off is the cost that comes with it.
lens.tactic: Evaluation and aggregation are too heavy to compute per request, so results are precomputed to keep reads fast.
lens.pattern: Implemented as about 30 precomputed tables filled by the nightly batch. Loads use DELETE→INSERT per snapshot_date: a same-day rerun overwrites, and each day accumulates. The web layer only reads.
lens.tradeoff: Data freshness depends on batch success. A failed batch leaves the previous day's values on screen, so batch monitoring and a "data as-of" date are required.

func.ingest: Vendors and POS provide only CSV, XLS and XLSX files, with no query API. 13 ingest batches are the only way data enters the system.
func.judge: Returns, transfers, samples, payout rate and order scores are calculated overnight. These analytical calculations (regression, percentiles, FIFO lot allocation) are kept off the request path.
func.order: Order sheets for 8 store types are generated in legacy .xls (BIFF), the format required by the downstream purchasing system.
func.console: An operations dashboard with 60 tabs in 13 groups, plus permission management.

qa.desc: Quality attributes are ranked so there is a clear rule for which one wins when two conflict.

accuracy.s: The same metric must return the same value in every tab. These values feed directly into purchase amounts and settlement.
accuracy.r: Single source of truth · shared formula modules · no duplicated evaluation logic

freshness.s: At the start of the workday, dashboards show data through the previous day's close along with the data as-of date.
freshness.r: Nightly precompute · batch run-history table · as-of date on screen

velocity.s: Approved changes to evaluation rules ship the same day. Frontend changes apply immediately without a restart.
velocity.r: Buildless · bind-mount deploy · per-tab isolation · three-layer split

readperf.s: Heavy evaluation tabs render immediately from precomputed data, with no recalculation.

ops.s: If the app fails, the container restarts automatically and checks the schema, keeping infrastructure work to a minimum.
ops.r: 2 nodes · 3 container types · restart: unless-stopped · automated deploy

qa.noscale: A few dozen internal users, 10 stores, and a few hundred thousand rows per day. Scalability was excluded from the quality goals so that effort went into accuracy and change velocity instead of the complexity scale-out requires (stateless services, distributed cache, external sessions, service decomposition).

const.desc: Fixed conditions at the start of the design, and how each one shaped it.

source.c: Vendors and POS provide data only as files (CSV · XLS · XLSX). No query API.
source.e: Ingest batches are the only entry point → the batch layer is the foundation of the system

output.c: The downstream purchasing system requires legacy .xls (BIFF)
output.e: xlwt is used and files are generated on the server

hw.c: Two self-hosted nodes (koclo-vm · NAS). No cloud budget.
hw.e: Vertical scaling only → designed around a single process and one DB per node

net.e: Outbound Cloudflare tunnel · self-hosted CI runner also dials out

biz.c: Evaluation rules (returns · transfers · samples · payout rate) change every season
biz.e: Frequent formula changes → deployment kept as simple as possible

verify.c: Existing review and test procedures validate changes before deployment
verify.e: Little need for build-time checks → no heavy build step

alt.desc: Alternatives were compared at three levels against the drivers: tactics are ways to achieve a quality attribute, styles define the overall system structure, and patterns are proven solutions to specific design problems.

tactic.desc: Design tactics chosen for each quality attribute.
tactic.time: Read performance — heavy computation moved from request time to the nightly batch.
tactic.ssot: Accuracy — a single database as the only integration point. No queue, RPC or shared file between batch and web, so values stay consistent.
tactic.idem: Data integrity — processing the same file more than once gives the same result, so recovery is a simple rerun.
tactic.obs: Observability — the four signals are collected on demand for a chosen target rather than continuously, and sessions expire automatically.

style.desc: Structural choices, and the alternatives that were ruled out.
style.layered: Each tab is split into three files: service (computation), router (JSON I/O) and Vue (UI). The server does not render HTML, and the UI layer does not compute.
style.cs: The SPA uses JSON APIs only. With no server templates, screen changes do not require a server restart.
style.pipeline: The batch and web layers run in separate processes, drivers and time windows, connected only through tables. A failure in one does not affect the other.
style.rejected: For a few dozen users and 10 stores, the cost of service decomposition and an event bus (boundary consistency, eventual consistency, distributed tracing) outweighed the benefit.

pattern.desc: Patterns applied to specific design problems.
pattern.read: Evaluation results are loaded into about 30 precomputed tables and the web layer only reads them. Write and read models are separated without event sourcing.
pattern.upsert: Three idempotent load methods, chosen by data type: ON CONFLICT upsert for accumulating time series, ranged DELETE+INSERT for sliding windows, and TRUNCATE and reload for current-state tables.
pattern.cache: Static files require server revalidation, and CSS and entry scripts are versioned with a ?v= stamp. Service worker caching is not used, to avoid conflicts with both.
pattern.tunnel: The host opens an outbound connection to receive domain traffic. Zero inbound ports and no certificate renewal. The CI runner dials out the same way.

runtime.desc: The nightly write flow and the daytime read flow use separate processes, drivers and time windows, and share only tables. A single integration point keeps values consistent, but a batch failure may not be visible on screen right away.

tradeoff.desc: Benefits and costs of each decision, identified by comparing alternatives.

pre.gain: Each tab query is a single indexed SELECT. Response time holds as screens are added, and per-date time-series tracking is available.
pre.cost: Data freshness depends on batch success. Logic changes require a rebuild, and foreign keys are kept minimal so tables can be regenerated (45 FKs across 150 tables).

build.gain: Frontend edits apply immediately with no rebuild or restart. Browser code matches the repository, so debugging works without source maps.
build.cost: No tree shaking or bundle splitting, so desktop views cannot be lazy-loaded. Type checks and linting run in the pre-merge process.

mount.gain: Deploys finish in seconds, with no build or push step in CI. Only reversible steps are automated.
mount.cost: No image-level rollback. Rollback is a git revert followed by a restart.

migrate.gain: No migration tool to learn, no version conflicts and no rollback scripts. Derived tables are dropped and regenerated.
migrate.cost: The schema source (init.sql) can drift from the live database, and with three apply paths it is hard to tell what has been applied.

proc.gain: The cache warmer, task worker and scheduler each run once. Prevents a failed reloader from continuing to serve old code.
proc.cost: Vertical scaling only, with brief downtime on restart. Heavy synchronous work has to be moved to a separate thread.

tunnel.gain: Zero inbound ports. No firewall, port forwarding or certificate renewal to manage, and TLS termination is handled externally.
tunnel.cost: The external service is a single point of failure. Without a proxy layer, static caching, rate limiting and IP allowlisting are handled in app middleware.

tradeoff.summary: Tool-provided functions — bundler optimization, migration ordering, CI regression checks — were replaced with development rules and procedures to increase development speed. As a result, development standards and the harness are managed as part of the architecture.

adr.desc: One record per decision. Each record covers context, alternatives, decision and consequences, with both benefits and costs listed under consequences.

a1.context: Input is vendor CSV, XLS and XLSX files, and the final output is a legacy .xls order sheet. Most of the processing in between is analytical (aggregation, weighted regression, percentiles, FIFO lot allocation) rather than CRUD, so most of the code sits in the data processing layer.
a1.alt: Choose a web framework first (Node or JVM) and fit data processing around it. This would mean building legacy .xls handling and analytics in-house or running them as a separate process.
a1.decision: The entire backend runs on Python + FastAPI. Data processing uses pandas, openpyxl, xlrd and xlwt, with a thin web layer on top.
a1.gain: Existing libraries for legacy .xls files are used as-is. API and batch share the same modules, so formulas such as backorder merging are maintained in one place.
a1.cost: The runtime is slower for CPU-bound work. Synchronous libraries (pandas, psycopg2) block the event loop unless moved to a separate thread.

a2.context: The UI is new to store staff, so feedback keeps coming in, and evaluation rules change each season — screens are updated often. Change quality is already covered by existing review and test procedures.
a2.alt: Adopt a bundler (Vite, webpack). This adds optimization and type checking, but the deployed output would differ from the source, requiring cache invalidation, deploy decisions and hotfix flow to be redesigned.
a2.decision: No bundler, node_modules or build step. Libraries load from CDN scripts and app code loads as native ES modules. This is a required rule in the development standard.
a2.gain: Frontend edits apply immediately without restart or rebuild. No Node toolchain versions, vulnerabilities or supply-chain risk to manage.
a2.cost: No tree shaking, bundle splitting or minification. Type checks and linting cannot be enforced in the deploy path, and module cache invalidation relies on server revalidation.

a3.context: ADR-002 had already fixed the buildless constraint. The screens include 60 tabs, nested sub-tabs, and large tables and charts with sort, filter, modal and selection state, and the earlier iframe approach had reached its limit.
a3.alt: React (requires JSX) · Angular (requires AOT compilation) · server templates with partial updates. The first two conflict with the buildless constraint, and the third struggles with this much UI state.
a3.decision: Vue 3 is loaded as the CDN global build, with components written as string templates in .js files. The global build includes the runtime template compiler, so components work without a build step.
a3.gain: SPA-level UI while keeping ADR-002. iframe tabs were migrated one at a time instead of a full rewrite.
a3.cost: Including the runtime compiler increases bundle size, and templates compile in the browser. String templates have no editor support or compile-time error checking.

a4.context: When the same number exists in both a file cache and the database, there is no clear source of truth, and screens show different values when only one side updates. Evaluation of returns, transfers, scores and payout rate is too heavy to compute per request, so both consistency and response time had to be met.
a4.alt: Keep the file cache alongside the DB (values can diverge) · compute on request (slow responses) · add a separate OLAP engine (too complex for the operations team size).
a4.decision: All data is consolidated into one PostgreSQL database, and the file cache is no longer a source of truth. The nightly batch loads heavy evaluation results into about 30 precomputed tables, and the web layer only reads them. DELETE→INSERT per snapshot_date provides same-day idempotency and per-date history.
a4.gain: Batch and web read the same data, so values no longer diverge. Tab queries are a single indexed SELECT, and daily history supports time-series tracking and later verification.
a4.cost: Freshness depends on batch success, so a failure shows previous values. Logic changes require a rebuild, and foreign keys are kept minimal for regeneration.

a5.context: Many of the 150 tables are derived or precomputed tables that can be regenerated, so a version-based migration tool offers little benefit. The operations team is also small.
a5.alt: Adopt a migration tool such as Alembic. This provides ordering and rollback scripts, but puts derived tables under version control and adds learning and operating cost.
a5.decision: No migration tool. The schema source is init.sql at the repository root, applied through three paths: init.sql on first run for a new DB; manual SQL files or ensure_schema() at app startup for existing DBs; and table creation inside some ingest batches.
a5.gain: No tool to learn, no version conflicts and no rollback scripts. With ensure_schema(), many changes apply automatically at startup after deploy.
a5.cost: The schema source can drift from the live DB, and three apply paths make status hard to check. Applying migrations before code is a manual step, supported by a hook that detects DDL execution.

a6.context: Deploys are frequent (2,054 commits), there is no container registry, and there are two target hosts with limited build capacity. Most changes are Python source or frontend files, and dependencies rarely change.
a6.alt: Rebuild the image and push to a registry on every deploy. This gives reproducible artifacts and rollback, but adds registry operations and build time to every deploy.
a6.decision: The image holds only dependencies, and app code is bind-mounted read-only from the host. Restarts are decided automatically by changed path: only backend/app/** triggers a restart, while dependency, image, compose and schema changes raise a warning for manual handling.
a6.gain: Deploys finish in seconds, and frontend changes need no restart. No build or push step keeps the CI pipeline simple.
a6.cost: No image-level rollback. Libraries present in the image but missing from the dependency list are hard to spot, and uncommitted changes on the host stop the deploy.

a7.context: With a few dozen internal users, multiple workers are not needed. The app process runs a cache warmer, task worker and scheduler, which would run multiple times with more workers, and the container mounts many NAS shares.
a7.alt: Multiple workers (gunicorn) with auto-reload. This adds throughput and convenience, but requires duplicate-run protection for background tasks, and a stopped file watcher can leave old code running.
a7.decision: uvicorn runs as a single process with auto-reload off. Code changes apply only through an explicit restart. On 2026-09-11 the second HTTPS process was removed, consolidating to one process.
a7.gain: Background tasks run exactly once. Prevents a failed reloader from continuing to serve old code.
a7.cost: Vertical scaling only, so throughput is limited to one core, with brief downtime on restart. One heavy synchronous task can slow all responses.

a8.context: Inbound ports cannot be opened on the production host, and there is no static IP or staff to manage certificates. Store staff still need mobile access from outside the office.
a8.alt: An nginx or caddy reverse proxy with open ports, port forwarding and automatic certificate renewal. This adds layered routing and static caching, but conflicts with the no-inbound constraint.
a8.decision: No reverse proxy. A Cloudflare tunnel connects outbound from the host and forwards domain traffic to localhost:9000. The CI runner connects out to GitHub from the host the same way.
a8.gain: Zero inbound ports. No firewall, port forwarding or certificate renewal to manage; TLS termination and DDoS mitigation are handled externally.
a8.cost: The external service is a single point of failure. Without a proxy layer, the app handles static caching, rate limiting and routing itself, including static file serving and IP allowlisting in middleware.

debt.desc: Technical debt resulting from the ADR decisions. When a review trigger occurs, the related ADR is revisited.

schema.w: Production DDL is copied back to the schema source manually, so the source can drift from the live DB. Three apply paths make status hard to check.
schema.s: When a new environment cannot be built from the schema source alone — reconsider a migration tool

fresh.w: A failed batch shows previous values instead of an error, so failures can go unnoticed.
fresh.s: When the as-of date or a failure alert does not reach users

load.w: Desktop views have no lazy loading, so the first visit downloads code for unused tabs. Code splitting is currently applied only to mobile views.
load.s: When slow initial loading is reported on store networks

verify.w: Verification happens before merge through four-dimension code review, a post-verification skill and verification scripts. The deploy pipeline does not re-check.
verify.s: When a change that skipped the process causes an incident — consider adding a verification step to the pipeline

layer.w: Most routers are thin, but some older ones contain SQL directly, blurring the line between computation and I/O.
layer.s: Move the logic to the service layer when that router is next modified

node.w: Both nodes run the same code but have separate databases. Both respond, so it can be unclear which node was queried.
node.s: When node confusion causes a wrong value check — fix the target node in the pipeline

debt.summary: Checks and ordering once handled by tools were replaced with development rules and procedures to increase speed, so development standards and the harness are managed as part of the architecture.

impact.consistency: A single database as the only integration point eliminated metric mismatches between tabs
impact.velocity: Buildless and bind-mount deploys apply frontend changes without restart and backend changes within seconds
impact.ops: Operations kept small with 2 nodes and 3 container types, with automated deploys, restart decisions and health checks
impact.trace: 8 decisions and 9 technical debt items recorded with ADRs and review triggers, keeping the design rationale traceable
